title: Risk and Return

text: Risk: The chance that an investment loses value or earns less than you expected. Investments with higher potential returns usually carry more risk.
title: Risk and Return

text: Compound interest: Earning returns on both your original money and the returns it has already earned. Over many years, this "interest on interest" can greatly increase your savings.
title: How Compound Interest Grows Your Money

text: Rule of 72: A shortcut for estimating how many years it takes money to double. Divide 72 by the yearly growth rate; at 8%, money doubles in about 9 years.
title: The Rule of 72

text: Inflation: The general rise in prices over time, which means each dollar buys a little less. Investments need to grow faster than inflation to increase your buying power.
title: Inflation and Your Money

text: Liquidity: How quickly and easily you can turn an investment into cash without losing value. A savings account is very liquid; a house is not.
title: Risk and Return

text: Time horizon: How long you plan to keep money invested before you need it. Longer time horizons usually allow for more risk.
title: Your Time Horizon

text: Dollar-cost averaging: Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule, no matter what prices are doing. You buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when they are high.
title: Dollar-Cost Averaging

text: Brokerage account: An account at a brokerage firm that lets you buy, hold and sell investments such as stocks, bonds and funds.
title: Types of Investment Accounts

text: Advisory fee: What you pay an investment adviser for managing your money or giving advice, often a percentage of your account each year.
title: Understanding Investment Fees

text: Security: A tradable financial investment, such as a stock, bond or fund share.
title: Five Questions to Ask Before You Invest

text: Stock: A share of ownership in a company. Stockholders can gain if the company's value rises and may receive dividends.
title: What Is a Stock?

text: Shareholder: A person or organization that owns shares of a company's stock.
title: What Is a Stock?

text: Dividend: A payment a company makes to its shareholders, usually from profits and often every quarter. Not all companies pay dividends, and they can be cut at any time.
title: Dividends

text: Dividend yield: A stock's yearly dividend divided by its price, shown as a percentage. A $100 stock paying $3 a year has a 3% dividend yield.
title: Dividends

text: Market capitalization: The total value of a company's shares, found by multiplying the share price by the number of shares. It is often shortened to "market cap."
title: Market Capitalization

text: Large-cap: A company with a large market capitalization, commonly over about $10 billion. Large-cap stocks tend to be more established and stable.
title: Market Capitalization

text: Small-cap: A company with a small market capitalization, commonly under about $2 billion. Small-cap stocks can grow faster but tend to swing more in price.
title: Market Capitalization

text: Growth stock: A stock in a company expected to grow sales and profits faster than average. These companies often reinvest profits instead of paying dividends.
title: Growth vs. Value Stocks

text: Value stock: A stock that looks inexpensive compared with measures like the company's earnings or assets. Value stocks are often established companies that pay dividends.
title: Growth vs. Value Stocks

text: Common stock: The most widely held type of stock, usually with voting rights. Common shareholders are paid last if a company goes bankrupt.
title: Common vs. Preferred Stock

text: Preferred stock: A type of stock that usually pays a fixed dividend before common shareholders are paid. It typically has no voting rights.
title: Common vs. Preferred Stock

text: Concentration risk: The risk of having too much money in one company, industry or investment. If that one holding struggles, your whole portfolio suffers.
title: The Risk of Owning Just a Few Stocks

text: Bond: A loan you make to a government or company. In return, it pays you interest and repays your money on a set date.
title: What Is a Bond?

text: Coupon: The interest rate a bond pays, usually twice a year. A $1,000 bond with a 4% coupon pays $40 a year.
title: What Is a Bond?

text: Face value: The amount a bond repays when it matures, often $1,000. It is also called par value.
title: What Is a Bond?

text: Maturity: The date a bond ends and the issuer repays its face value.
title: What Is a Bond?

text: Yield: The income an investment produces, shown as a percentage. For bonds, yield rises when the price falls, and falls when the price rises.
title: Bond Yield

text: Yield to maturity: The total yearly return you can expect if you hold a bond until it matures, including interest and any gain or loss from the price you paid.
title: Bond Yield

text: Interest rate risk: The risk that a bond's price falls because interest rates rise. Longer-term bonds are affected more.
title: Why Bond Prices Fall When Interest Rates Rise

text: Credit rating: A grade from a rating agency showing how likely a bond issuer is to pay its interest and repay the loan.
title: Bond Credit Ratings

text: Investment grade: A bond with a higher credit rating, meaning the issuer is considered more likely to pay. These bonds usually pay less interest than lower-rated ones.
title: Bond Credit Ratings

text: High-yield bond: A bond with a lower credit rating that pays more interest to make up for a higher chance of default. It is sometimes called a junk bond.
title: Corporate and High-Yield Bonds

text: Default: When a borrower, such as a bond issuer, fails to make promised interest or principal payments.
title: Corporate and High-Yield Bonds

text: Treasury bill: A short-term loan to the U.S. government that matures in one year or less. It is sold below face value, and you receive the full face value at maturity.
title: U.S. Treasury Securities

text: TIPS: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, U.S. government bonds whose principal rises and falls with inflation.
title: U.S. Treasury Securities

text: I bond: A U.S. savings bond whose interest rate combines a fixed rate and an inflation rate that resets every six months. It must be held for at least one year.
title: I Bonds

text: Municipal bond: A bond issued by a state, city or other local government. Its interest is often exempt from federal income tax.
title: Municipal Bonds

text: Mutual fund: A fund that pools money from many investors to buy a collection of stocks, bonds or other investments. It is priced once a day at its net asset value.
title: What Is a Mutual Fund?

text: ETF: An exchange-traded fund, a basket of investments that trades on a stock exchange like a single stock. Many ETFs track an index at a low cost.
title: What Is an ETF?

text: Index fund: A mutual fund or ETF that aims to match a market index, like the S&P 500, instead of trying to beat it. Index funds usually have low fees.
title: Index Funds

text: Expense ratio: The yearly fee a fund charges, shown as a percentage of your investment. A 0.50% expense ratio costs about $50 a year per $10,000 invested.
title: Expense Ratios

text: Sales load: A commission some mutual funds charge when you buy or sell shares. Funds without one are called no-load funds.
title: Sales Loads and 12b-1 Fees

text: 12b-1 fee: An ongoing yearly fee some mutual funds charge to pay for marketing and distribution. It is included in the fund's expense ratio.
title: Sales Loads and 12b-1 Fees

text: Net asset value: The price of one mutual fund share, calculated once a day by dividing the fund's assets minus its debts by the number of shares. It is often shortened to NAV.
title: Net Asset Value (NAV)

text: Target date fund: A fund that holds a mix of stocks and bonds and becomes more conservative as a chosen year, usually your retirement year, gets closer.
title: Target Date Funds

text: Glide path: The planned schedule a target date fund follows to shift from stocks toward bonds and cash over time.
title: Target Date Funds

text: Money market fund: A mutual fund that invests in very short-term, high-quality debt and aims to keep a stable value. Unlike a bank deposit, it is not FDIC insured.
title: Money Market Funds

text: Active management: An approach where fund managers pick investments to try to beat the market. Actively managed funds usually charge higher fees.
title: Active vs. Passive Funds

text: Passive investing: An approach that tracks a market index instead of picking investments, usually through low-cost index funds.
title: Active vs. Passive Funds

text: Prospectus: A document that describes a fund or other investment, including its goals, risks and fees. Reading it before you invest helps you know what you are buying.
title: What Is a Mutual Fund?

text: 401(k): A retirement savings plan offered by an employer that lets you invest part of each paycheck with tax advantages. Many employers add a matching contribution.
title: 401(k) Plans

text: Employer match: Money your employer adds to your retirement plan when you contribute, usually up to a set percentage of your salary.
title: Employer Matching Contributions

text: Vesting: The schedule that determines when your employer's contributions become fully yours. Money you contribute yourself is always fully vested.
title: Employer Matching Contributions

text: Traditional IRA: An individual retirement account where contributions may be tax-deductible and withdrawals in retirement are taxed as income.
title: Traditional IRAs

text: Roth IRA: An individual retirement account funded with after-tax money, where qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
title: Roth IRAs

text: Tax-deferred: Taxes on contributions and growth are postponed until you withdraw the money, as in a traditional 401(k) or IRA.
title: Traditional vs. Roth

text: Catch-up contribution: An extra amount people aged 50 or older can contribute to retirement accounts each year, above the regular limit.
title: 2026 Retirement Contribution Limits

text: Required minimum distribution: The minimum amount you must withdraw each year from certain retirement accounts, such as traditional IRAs, generally starting at age 73. It is often shortened to RMD.
title: Traditional vs. Roth

text: Early withdrawal penalty: The 10% additional tax usually charged on retirement account withdrawals before age 59½, on top of income tax. Some exceptions apply.
title: Early Withdrawals from Retirement Accounts

text: Health savings account: A tax-advantaged account for medical expenses, available with a qualifying high-deductible health plan. It is often shortened to HSA.
title: Health Savings Accounts (HSAs)

text: High-deductible health plan: A health insurance plan with a higher deductible that meets IRS rules. You need one to contribute to a health savings account.
title: Health Savings Accounts (HSAs)

text: Capital gain: The profit from selling an investment for more than you paid for it. In a taxable account, capital gains are taxed when you sell.
title: Capital Gains Taxes

text: Long-term capital gain: A profit on an investment held more than one year. It is taxed at lower rates than regular income.
title: Capital Gains Taxes

text: Short-term capital gain: A profit on an investment held one year or less. It is taxed at your regular income tax rate.
title: Capital Gains Taxes

text: Capital loss: The loss from selling an investment for less than you paid. Capital losses can offset capital gains and up to $3,000 of other income a year.
title: Capital Gains Taxes

text: Portfolio: All the investments you own, taken together.
title: Building a Simple Portfolio

text: Diversification: Spreading your money across many different investments so that one poor performer doesn't sink your whole portfolio.
title: Diversification

text: Asset allocation: How you divide your money among types of investments, mainly stocks, bonds and cash. Your mix shapes both your potential returns and your risk.
title: Asset Allocation

text: Rebalancing: Adjusting your portfolio to bring it back to your target mix after market moves have shifted it.
title: Rebalancing

text: Risk tolerance: How much ups and downs in your investments you are willing and able to handle. Finnie uses three levels, Conservative, Moderate and Aggressive.
title: Risk Tolerance

text: Volatility: How much and how quickly an investment's price moves up and down. Higher volatility means bigger swings.
title: Volatility

text: Diversification score: Finnie's 0 to 100 measure of how spread out your portfolio is. A single stock scores 0; a mix of broad funds scores high.
title: Diversification

text: Three-fund portfolio: A simple portfolio built from three broad index funds, usually U.S. stocks, international stocks and U.S. bonds.
title: Building a Simple Portfolio

text: Stock exchange: A marketplace where shares of public companies are bought and sold, such as the New York Stock Exchange or Nasdaq.
title: How the Stock Market Works

text: Market index: A measure that tracks the performance of a group of investments, giving a snapshot of part of the market.
title: Market Indexes

text: S&P 500: A market index of about 500 large U.S. companies, widely used as a measure of the overall U.S. stock market.
title: Market Indexes

text: Bull market: A period of rising prices and optimism, commonly defined as a rise of 20% or more from a recent low.
title: Bull and Bear Markets

text: Bear market: A period of falling prices and pessimism, commonly defined as a drop of 20% or more from a recent high.
title: Bull and Bear Markets

text: Correction: A market decline of about 10% from a recent high. Corrections are more common than bear markets.
title: Bull and Bear Markets

text: Market order: An order to buy or sell right away at the best available price. It almost always fills, but you don't control the exact price.
title: Market Orders and Limit Orders

text: Limit order: An order to buy or sell only at a price you set or better. You control the price, but the order may never fill.
title: Market Orders and Limit Orders

text: Bid: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay for a stock or other security.
title: How Your Trade Gets Executed

text: Ask: The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept for a stock or other security.
title: How Your Trade Gets Executed

text: Spread: The difference between the bid and the ask price. Heavily traded stocks usually have very small spreads.
title: How Your Trade Gets Executed

text: Federal Reserve: The central bank of the United States. It sets monetary policy, which influences interest rates across the economy.
title: Interest Rates and the Federal Reserve

text: Federal funds rate: The interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Federal Reserve sets a target for it, which affects many other rates.
title: Interest Rates and the Federal Reserve

text: Emergency fund: Money set aside for unexpected costs like car repairs or a job loss. A common goal is three to six months of essential expenses.
title: Building an Emergency Fund

text: High-yield savings account: A savings account that pays a higher interest rate than a typical bank savings account. Many are offered by online banks.
title: Savings Accounts and FDIC Insurance

text: FDIC insurance: Federal protection for bank deposits, up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category. It does not cover investments like stocks or funds.
title: Savings Accounts and FDIC Insurance

text: Certificate of deposit: A bank deposit that pays a fixed rate for a set term. Taking money out early usually costs a penalty. It is often shortened to CD.
title: Saving for Short-Term Goals

text: APR: Annual percentage rate, the yearly cost of borrowing money, such as on a credit card. A high APR makes paying off that debt a strong first step before investing.
title: Paying Off High-Interest Debt First
